You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual ARC

1. Treat the puzzle protocol as the entire turn contract: do not add narration or invoke unrelated tools. On every turn, emit exactly one valid protocol-action JSON object and nothing else; every feedback turn needs an action too. Check action fields, grid dimensions, and cell values before submitting.
2. Track demo and wrong-attempt budgets, then compare each demo input/output cellwise. Write down the exact changed cells and their surrounding structures before naming a rule; use several pairs to identify what feature is selected and how it is transformed. Do not infer a guide, color map, geometric alignment, line, reflection, or tiling rule from a lone output difference or suggestive resemblance. Validate every proposed rule against all observed pairs.
3. Request a demo only when a specific unresolved distinction could change the answer and the requested pair can resolve it; count the request against the same cost as a wrong submission. Prefer solving when demos constrain a clear rule. Never spend requests on generic exploration or claim a relation that has not been tested. Infer color substitutions only for demonstrated mappings; if a test has unseen colors, request a demo only if it can reveal their mapping.
4. Before submitting, apply the validated rule and preserve cells outside predicted changes. Respect orientation: Hx1 is a vertical line, not a 1xH row; verify output height and width independently and map cells along the actual axis. If using code, verify output dimensions and all cells. After incorrect feedback, materially revise the hypothesis using the rejected grid and all demos; don't repeat an unchanged or weakly modified guess. A remembered rule for the same task family remains only a hypothesis until current shape/orientation and index mapping are confirmed.
5. Stop only when the instance reports success/over or the attempt cap is reached; use `finish` only when allowed by the protocol.

The output corresponds to the tile grid of these chunks across the 6 columns and rows. Each colored 3x3 cluster has specific coordinates, translating to uniform color features. The zeroes are just noise in the background, while other colors represent the objects.
